title: Pure Pairs, Forests and Path–Antipath Classes

items.title: The strong Erdős–Hajnal property for a hereditary graph class
Every nontrivial $P_4$-free graph is disconnected or has disconnected complement
items.strategy: Record the Seinsche cograph characterization in the form used by Bousquet-Lagoutte-Thomasse: a nontrivial graph with no induced $P_4$ cannot be both connected and anticonnected. This is the structural input behind the strong-to-weak Erdős-Hajnal implication.

items.title: Every $P_4$-free graph has a clique or stable set of size at least the square root of its order
items.strategy: Induct on the number of vertices using the previous disconnected-or-antidisconnected dichotomy. In the disconnected case combine maxima across components; in the complement-disconnected case apply the same argument to stable sets.

items.title: The strong Erdős–Hajnal property implies the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Follow Bousquet-Lagoutte-Thomasse's induction: the strong property recursively builds a large induced cograph by splitting along a complete or anticomplete pair, and the square-root bound for $P_4$-free graphs then yields the required polynomial clique-or-stable-set bound.

items.title: Every $H$-free graph has a polynomial-size pure pair
items.strategy: Record the Erdős-Hajnal-Pach bipartite analogue as the general pure-pair baseline: the source's candidate-set embedding argument forces a large complete or anticomplete pair whenever the forbidden induced pattern is fixed.

items.title: For every $k$, the class forbidding $P_k$ and $\overline{P_k}$ has the strong Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Use the Bousquet-Lagoutte-Thomasse route: the earlier Rödl/Fox-Sudakov family corollary supplies a large restricted induced subgraph, and the source's connected-case lemma then forces a linear biclique in the graph or its complement.

items.title: For every $k$, the class forbidding $P_k$ and $\overline{P_k}$ has the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Apply the strong-to-weak implication to the hereditary class from the previous theorem.

items.title: Every forest-free graph has a linear anticomplete pair or a linear-degree vertex
items.strategy: Record the main sparse theorem from Pure pairs I: in an $H$-free graph for a fixed forest $H$, either some vertex has linear degree or there are two large anticomplete sets. This is the source endpoint that the forest pure-pair theorem is derived from.

items.title: For every forest $H$, graphs excluding $H$ and $\overline{H}$ have a linear pure pair
items.strategy: Use the source's derivation from the preceding sparse theorem together with complement symmetry to package a linear complete or anticomplete pair for graphs excluding a forest and its complement.

items.title: For every forest $H$, graphs excluding $H$ and $\overline{H}$ have the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Apply the strong-to-weak implication to the previous forest pure-pair theorem.

items.title: Co-leaves of a finite graph
Deleting a leaf from each of two forbidden graphs preserves virality
items.strategy: Use Nguyen-Scott-Seymour's unordered leaf-deletion theorem: if the two smaller families obtained by deleting the chosen leaves are viral, then the original family is viral.

items.title: Deleting a leaf and a co-leaf preserves virality of a finite forbidden family
items.strategy: Translate the co-leaf side into a leaf in the complement and then use the earlier leaf-deletion theorem, with Huang-Ju-Zhou's Theorem 1.7 fixing the exact family notation that later E-graph deductions use.

items.title: Deleting a leaf and a co-leaf preserves the Erdős–Hajnal property of a finite forbidden family
items.strategy: Combine the virality preservation theorem with the finite-family equivalence between the Erdős-Hajnal property and virality.

title: Pure Pairs, Forests and Path–Antipath Classes — Examples

items.title: The path-antipath theorem specialized to $P_5$ and $\overline{P_5}$
items.strategy: Instantiate the path-antipath Erdős-Hajnal theorem at $k=5$ and identify the two forbidden graphs using the library's standard path notation.

items.title: The forest pure-pair theorem specialized to $P_4$
items.strategy: Note that $P_4$ is a forest and is isomorphic to its complement, so the forest-complement theorem applies to the cograph case without changing the forbidden graph.

items.title: A co-leaf of $\overline{P_5}$ is exactly a leaf of $P_5$
items.strategy: Label the five-vertex path in order, compute the degrees in its complement, and check that the two degree-three vertices of $\overline{P_5}$ are precisely the images of the two leaves of $P_5$.

items.title: The leaf/co-leaf corollary recovers the $P_5$ case from the $P_4$ case
items.strategy: Apply the leaf/co-leaf Erdős-Hajnal corollary to the family $\{P_5,\overline{P_5}\}$: deleting a leaf on each side leaves $\{P_4,\overline{P_4}\}$, and the previous example identifies that smaller family with the cograph case.

items.title: The mixed-block reachability relation on a blockade
Mixed-block reachability is an equivalence relation
items.strategy: The relation is reflexive by definition, symmetric because mixedness is symmetric for unordered pairs of disjoint sets, and transitive by concatenating mixed block chains.

items.title: The quotient blockade obtained from mixed-block reachability
A quotient block of connected or anticonnected blocks is again connected or anticonnected
items.strategy: Induct along a mixed block chain. Mixedness gives at least one edge between consecutive connected blocks and at least one nonedge between consecutive anticonnected blocks, so connectivity in the graph or its complement survives each union.

items.title: Blocks from distinct mixed-block classes are pure to each other
items.strategy: If two blocks in different classes were mixed, that mixed edge would itself be a length-one witness putting them in the same reachability class.

items.title: A vertex mixed on a quotient block but pure on each member block yields two mixed member blocks with opposite adjacency
items.strategy: Choose member blocks on which the external vertex is complete and anticomplete, then walk along a mixed chain inside the quotient class until the adjacency switches for the first time.

items.title: A quotient-level mixed-block witness descends to two mixed member blocks
items.strategy: Apply the previous two lemmas inside the first mixed quotient block: the no-mixing hypothesis on the other quotient block forces the needed mixed vertex to come from that side, and its two opposite adjacencies descend to member blocks.

title: Quotient Blockades and Mixing Relations — Examples

items.title: Mixedness of block pairs is not transitive
items.strategy: Exhibit three disjoint blocks $A,B,C$ with $(A,B)$ and $(B,C)$ mixed but $(A,C)$ anticomplete. This shows why the quotient page uses the reachability closure of mixedness rather than mixedness itself.

items.title: A mixed chain of blocks collapses to one quotient block
items.strategy: Take a four-block blockade in which consecutive pairs are mixed and the end pair is pure; compute the reachability classes explicitly and verify that the quotient merges exactly the chain component.

items.title: A vertex may be mixed on a quotient block while pure on each member block
items.strategy: Choose two mixed member blocks inside one quotient class and an external vertex complete to one but anticomplete to the other. Their union is then mixed to that vertex although each member block is still pure to it.

items.title: The quotient-witness reduction in a four-block configuration
items.strategy: Write down a four-block example with two quotient classes and vertices $x,y,u$ satisfying the quotient-level hypotheses, then track the reduction to concrete member blocks $A_1,A_2$ as in Lemma 6.2.
